aer.def: Annual Equivalent Rate: a savings rate including compounding over a year, so you can compare accounts fairly.

apprentice wage.def: Pay for an apprentice: at least the apprentice minimum (£8.00 an hour from April 2026) under 19 or in the first year, then the rate for your age.

apr.def: Annual Percentage Rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and compulsory fees. Lower is cheaper.

asset.def: Something you own that's worth money: savings, shares, a car, a house.

auto-enrolment.def: The law that makes employers put eligible staff (22+, earning over £10,000) into a workplace pension automatically.

bank of england.def: The UK's central bank. It sets Bank Rate and aims to keep inflation at 2%.

bank rate.def: The Bank of England's main interest rate. Savings and borrowing rates across the UK tend to follow it.

bills.def: Regular household costs such as energy, water, broadband, phone and insurance. Budget for each as a monthly amount.

bnpl.def: Splitting a purchase into a few payments, often interest-free. It's still debt, and missed payments can hurt your credit file.

budget.def: A plan for your money: what comes in, what goes out on needs and wants, and what's left to save.

cash isa.def: A savings account inside an ISA wrapper, so the interest is tax-free.

compound interest.def: Interest that's added to your balance, so next time you earn interest on the interest too.

council tax.def: A yearly charge per home paid to the local council. 25% off if you live alone; full-time students are usually exempt.

cpi.def: The Consumer Prices Index: the main UK measure of inflation, worked out by the ONS from the prices of a basket of everyday items.

credit file.def: Your record of borrowing and repayments, kept by Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Lenders check it when you apply.

credit score.def: A number an agency or app works out from your credit file. Lenders use your file and their own rules, not this number.

current account.def: Your everyday bank account for pay coming in and bills and card payments going out. Usually pays little or no interest.

deflation.def: Prices in general falling over time.

easy-access account.def: A savings account you can pay into and take money from at any time. The rate is usually variable.

emergency fund.def: Easy-access savings kept for the unexpected. Guidance suggests three to six months of essential costs.

employer contribution.def: Money your employer pays into your pension on top of your pay. At least 3% of qualifying earnings under auto-enrolment.

fixed-rate saver.def: A savings account (often called a bond) that locks your money away for a set time at a fixed rate.

fscs.def: The Financial Services Compensation Scheme: pays back savers up to £120,000 per person per banking licence if a UK bank fails.

gross pay.def: What you earn before anything is taken off: your salary or hourly rate times hours.

inflation.def: The rate at which prices in general rise over time, so the same £1 buys less.

interest.def: The price of using money. Savers earn it and borrowers pay it.

interest rate.def: Interest as a percentage of the principal. Nearly always quoted per year.

isa.def: Individual Savings Account: a tax-free wrapper for cash or investments. Nothing inside is taxed.

isa allowance.def: The most you can pay into ISAs in a tax year: £20,000 in 2026/27, across all types. Use it or lose it.

junior isa.def: A tax-free account for under-18s, opened by a parent or guardian. The child gets it at 18.

lifetime isa.def: An ISA for a first home or later life: open at 18–39, pay in up to £4,000 a year, get a 25% bonus. A 25% charge applies to other withdrawals.

marginal rate.def: The rate charged on your next pound of income. Higher than your average rate, because lower slices of pay are taxed less.

market.def: Anywhere buyers and sellers meet to agree a price.

minimum payment trap.def: Paying only a card's minimum, so most of each payment is interest and the debt lasts for years.

money.def: Anything people accept in exchange for goods and services. In the UK that's pounds, mostly held as numbers in bank accounts rather than notes and coins.

national insurance.def: A deduction from pay over a threshold that builds your record for the State Pension and some benefits.

net pay.def: Take-home pay: what reaches your bank account after tax, National Insurance, pension and any student loan.

nominal return.def: The return shown on your statement, before taking inflation into account.

overdraft.def: Borrowing by letting your current account go below £0. Arranged overdrafts often cost around 40% a year.

paye.def: Pay As You Earn: your employer works out your income tax and National Insurance and pays it to HMRC each time you're paid.

payslip.def: The statement you get each payday showing gross pay, every deduction and net pay.

personal allowance.def: The income you can have each tax year before paying income tax: £12,570 for most people in 2026/27.

principal.def: The amount you start with, before any interest is added.

real return.def: What you gain in spending power after inflation. Roughly the nominal rate minus inflation; exactly (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

rent.def: What you pay a landlord to live in a home. In England, deposits are capped at five weeks' rent and must be protected.

rule of 72.def: A shortcut: 72 ÷ the yearly rate ≈ how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years.

self-assessment.def: The yearly tax return for income HMRC doesn't already tax through PAYE, such as self-employed profit over £1,000.

simple interest.def: Interest worked out only on the original principal, so it's the same every year.

sipp.def: Self-Invested Personal Pension: a pension you open and manage yourself, with the same tax relief.

state pension.def: A regular payment from the government from State Pension age, based on your National Insurance record.

stocks and shares isa.def: An ISA that holds investments such as funds and shares. Gains and dividends are tax-free; the value can fall.

student loan plans.def: The repayment rules for your loan. Plan 5 (England, courses from 2023): 9% of income above £25,000, written off after 40 years.

tax code.def: Tells your employer how much tax-free pay you get. 1257L means £12,570 a year, the standard Personal Allowance.

tax relief.def: Income tax given back on pension contributions, so each £1 in your pot costs a basic-rate taxpayer about 80p.

trading allowance.def: Up to £1,000 a year of income from self-employment or side hustles that you don't need to declare or pay tax on.

variable rate.def: An interest rate the bank can change at any time. Most easy-access savings accounts have one.

workplace pension.def: A pension your employer sets up, which you and your employer pay into while you work.
